rejected.title: Experiences and perspectives in the Holocaust
card: Victims
Jewish people, and others the Nazis targeted, suffered persecution and murder. Their diaries, letters and survivor testimony show what it was like to live through it.
Perpetrators
These were the people who carried out the persecution and killing. This included officials, police and soldiers as well as camp guards.
Bystanders
These were people who saw what was happening but did not act, or did little. Some feared punishment, some did not care and some gained from the situation.
Resisters and rescuers
Some people fought back or helped others, often at great risk. Examples are Jewish uprisings in ghettos and people who hid Jewish families.
rejected.remember: Historians compare many groups and ask why people acted as they did.

a.q: A historian reads a diary written by a Jewish girl hiding in Amsterdam. Whose experience does this source show?
opts: A victim of the Holocaust
A perpetrator of the Holocaust
A bystander to the Holocaust
A rescuer during the Holocaust
a.why: The diary writer was a Jewish person persecuted by the Nazis, so it shows a victim's experience. It is not a rescuer's view, even though rescuers helped her hide, because she is the one writing about her own life.
a.clue: Who is the person writing about their own life?

b.q: Tomas lived next door to a Jewish family in a Polish town. He watched them taken away and said nothing, because he feared being punished. How would a historian describe him?
opts: A bystander, who saw but did not act
A perpetrator, who carried out the arrests
A rescuer, who risked his life to help
A victim, who was targeted by the Nazis
b.why: Tomas saw what happened and did not act, which makes him a bystander. His fear explains why he stayed silent, but it does not make him a perpetrator, because he did not carry out the arrests.
b.clue: Did Tomas take part in the persecution or try to stop it?

version.title: Experiences and perspectives in the Holocaust
card: Victims
Jewish people, and others the Nazis targeted such as Roma and disabled people, were persecuted and murdered. Their diaries, letters and survivors' accounts show what they lived through.
Perpetrators

People who carried out the persecution and killing, from officials who organised it to police, soldiers and camp guards. Historians study their orders and trial records to ask why they took part, such as belief in Nazi ideas, obeying orders or wanting to fit in.
Bystanders
People who saw what was happening and did nothing or little. Some were afraid of punishment, some did not care, and some gained, such as by taking Jewish homes or jobs.
Resisters and rescuers
People who fought back or helped others, often at the risk of death. Jews rose up in the Warsaw ghetto in 1943, and some non-Jews hid Jewish families in their homes.
version.remember: Historians ask what each person lived through and why they made the choices they did.

a.q: Historians find that some bystanders stayed silent out of fear, some did not care, and some gained. What does this show?
opts: People in one group could act for different reasons
Every bystander secretly agreed with the Nazis' ideas
Bystanders stayed silent only because they were afraid
Historians can never know why any bystander acted
a.why: The same group held people with different reasons, which is why historians ask about each person's choices. Fear was one reason, but not the only one, and not every bystander shared Nazi beliefs.
a.clue: Count how many different reasons the question gives.

b.q: Hans, a German clerk, typed the lists of Jewish families to be sent to the camps. He later said he was only doing his job. How would a historian describe his role?
opts: A perpetrator, as his work helped carry out the killing
A bystander, as he never harmed anyone with his own hands
A victim, as he was made to do the job against his will
A rescuer, as he could warn families before they were taken
b.why: Officials who organised the persecution are perpetrators, because their work made the killing possible. Hans did not kill anyone himself, but he took part rather than only watching, so he was not a bystander.
b.clue: Think about what his lists were used for.

a.best: People in one group could act for different reasons

b.best: A perpetrator, as his work helped carry out the killing

problems.detail: The right option is the only one with a hedge ("could"), while all three wrong options use absolutes ("Every", "only", "never"). A test-wise student could pick it by dropping the absolutes without knowing the idea.

check.summary: The facts are right and both intended answers are correct. One small wording issue: in question a, the right option is the only one without an absolute word, so a student could guess it.

a.q: Historians find that some bystanders stayed silent out of fear, some did not care, and some gained. What does this show?
